extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Describes and analyzes the principal affirmative and negative defenses available to defendants in U.S. patent-infringement suits (repeal/surrender/title, non-coverage, non-infringing acts, timing, co-ownership/license, statutes of limitation), with case-law illustrations and limits on each defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixteenth Defence: Repeal of the Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the patent, though issued in apparent conformity with the requirements of the law, ever existed as a lawful patent, or still exists in any form whatever; equivalent to an averment that the patent was granted contrary to law and has been recalled and cancelled by the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent has been revoked (by a rival patentee in equitable proceedings or by the government) it is held void ab initio and the monopoly is treated as having never existed; this defence is available in any suit based on the patent when repeal is total. If annulment was limited (as to certain owners or territory), the patent may remain in force as to others and the defence will not bar actions by unaffected owners. (Surrounding explanation: distinguishes surrender/extinction of rights vs. repeal/annulment making patent void ab initio; cites illustrations and related sections.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventeenth Defence: Denial of a Legal Title in the Plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: Attacks the plaintiff’s legal title to the patent — a denial that his interest in the patented invention is sufficient to enable him to maintain an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence targets defects in the legal ownership/assignment/territorial rights (patentee, assignee, grantee enforcing within territory). Matters of corporate capacity, infancy, coverture, misjoinder/non-joinder are not part of this defence but are available in abatement. Equitable interests cannot be asserted in a legal action to defeat the record owner’s claims. (Examples/cases cited to illustrate limits.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighteenth Defence: Denial that the Art or Instrument Employed by the Defendant is Covered by the Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the art or article employed by the defendant is covered by the plaintiff’s patent — i.e., the idea or means embodied in the defendant’s invention is not identical with or included in the idea embodied in the plaintiff’s claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not merely a denial of identity: an original invention may be infringed by an improvement. The defence must show the defendant’s invention excludes the patented invention in every form to avoid liability; if the defendant’s device uses the plaintiff’s invention alone or as an element or foundation (even if combined with improvements), infringement may still be found. (Cites §¶ and cases discussing identity vs. inclusion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nineteenth Defence: Denial that the Acts of the Defendant were Infringing Acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the acts performed by the defendant were of such a character as to subject him to an action for infringement — i.e., averment that he has not voluntarily made, used, or sold the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains judicial construction of 'make', 'use', and 'sell' (broadly construed to include artifices to achieve same results) and when the conduct fails to meet those constructions. Appropriate where defendant’s conduct does not fall within the interpreted meanings or where acts were not voluntary (workmen, agents, officials acting under orders with no discretion), in which case legal imputation may rest on superiors rather than the actor. (References sections detailing forms of infringing acts and controlling cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Twentieth Defence: Denial that the Alleged Acts were Committed while the Patent was in Force
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the patent was in force when the alleged acts of infringement were committed — concedes the acts but avers they occurred before issuance or after expiration of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement under U.S. law requires acts committed while the patent creates the right; acts before grant or after expiration are generally not actionable as patent infringement (though pre-grant/common-law remedies may exist). Exception where post-expiration acts relate back to preparations made during patent life, constituting a single transaction. Patent term on its face is not always conclusive; where prior foreign patents exist for same invention, domestic patent life may be measured by the foreign patent which first expires. (Cites sections and cases on relation-back, measurement of term, and timing disputes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-First Defence: Co-ownership of the Patent or License from its Lawful Owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Averment that the defendant’s making, using, or selling the invention was not wrongful because he acted with due authority — e.g., as a part-owner or as a licensee of the lawful owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper where a part-owner is sued by a co-owner for acts confined to employment of the patented invention, or where a licensee acts within license scope. If the part-owner or licensee practices an invention that is not identical to the patented invention (or exceeds license scope), the defence will not avail — such acts may be true infringements. License revocation timing and limits of authority (acts beyond license) are relevant; a licensee may still infringe by acts not covered by the license. (Illustrative cases and cross-references provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-Second Defence: Statute of Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Averment that the plaintiff has not commenced his action within the time prescribed by the Statute of Limitations; this defence rests on estoppel doctrines and asserts forfeiture of remedy by plaintiff conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion of complexity whether state statutes of limitation apply to federal patent suits (divergent authority). Notes the historical federal statute (act of July 8, 1870 / Sec. 55) that required actions within patent term or six years after expiration (later omitted from the Revised Statutes), and the conflicts about its scope and repeal. Courts differ on whether state limitation statutes apply when no federal statute governs; arguments about federal uniformity and congressional power to set limitations are summarized. The defence’s applicability depends on statutory history, whether acts accrued while statute in force, prospective/retroactive operation, and relevant case law citations and commentary.
